<explanation>
Below is a step-by-step guide for drawing a system design diagram tailored to the CLI Agent Orchestrator (CAO) project. Follow these instructions to capture all essential architectural elements and relationships.

1. Identify Project Type and Purpose
   - CAO is a command-line, multi-agent orchestration system built in Python.  
   - It manages collaborative AI “agents” via tmux sessions and an HTTP MCP (Model Context Protocol) server.  
   - Primary use cases: hierarchical task delegation, parallel/ sequential workflows, scheduled flows.

2. Analyze File Structure
   - Top-level folders:
     • src/cli_agent_orchestrator – core Python package  
       – cli/commands & cli/main.py – command-line interface  
       – mcp_server/ – HTTP server, REST API, models, routing  
       – api/ – CLI exposes its own internal API commands  
       – clients/ – tmux and database drivers  
       – services/ – business logic for sessions, flows, inbox, cleanup  
       – providers/ – adapters for external LLM-in-CLI tools (Claude Code, Amazon Q)  
       – models/ – domain objects (AgentProfile, Session, Flow, Inbox)  
       – utils/ – shared utilities (logging, templates, terminal helpers)  
   - Other files:
     • tmux-install.sh, pyproject.toml, uv.lock – build/deploy config  
     • docs/ & examples/ – architecture diagrams, API spec, sample workflows.

3. Examine README Insights
   - Central components described: CLI front-end, local MCP HTTP server, tmux session manager, agent store.  
   - Core orchestration patterns: handoff (sync), assign (async), send_message (inbox).  
   - Flows subsystem: cron-like scheduler that posts jobs to the MCP server.

4. Main Components to Draw
   A. CLI (cao, cao-server, cao flow)
     – User invokes CLI commands  
     – CLI calls internal Python modules in src/cli_agent_orchestrator/cli  
   B. MCP Server (HTTP service on localhost:9889)
     – Endpoints: session management, messaging, flow management  
     – Implements REST API via src/cli_agent_orchestrator/mcp_server/server.py  
     – Persists state via clients/database.py  
   C. tmux Controller
     – tmux client wrapper in clients/tmux.py  
     – Creates/tears down isolated sessions/windows per agent  
   D. Agent Processes
     – Each tmux window runs an “agent” Python process with unique CAO_TERMINAL_ID  
     – Agents communicate with the MCP Server via MCP tools (handoff, assign, send_message)  
   E. Agent Store & Profiles
     – Markdown agent profiles under src/.../agent_store or ~/.aws/...  
     – Template loader in utils/template.py  
   F. Workflow Scheduler (Flows)
     – Flow service (services/flow_service.py) reads cron configs  
     – Posts tasks to MCP server for execution  
   G. External Provider Adapters
     – Claude Code, Amazon Q, CLI-based LLM providers under providers/  
     – Wrap API calls, inject into agent sessions

5. Relationships & Data Flows
   1. User → CLI  
   2. CLI → MCP Server (HTTP REST)  
   3. MCP Server ↔ Database (state: sessions, inbox, flows)  
   4. MCP Server → tmux client (spawn new sessions or send commands)  
   5. tmux agent processes → MCP Server (via REST calls)  
      – Handoff, assign, send_message tools embed HTTP calls  
   6. Scheduler (flows) → MCP Server → tmux  
   7. Agents ↔ Agents via MCP Server inbox

6. Architectural Patterns & Design Principles
   - Separation of Concerns: CLI front-end, API server, session orchestration, persistence, adapters  
   - Modular layering: cli → api → services → clients  
   - Isolation pattern: one tmux session per agent for context separation  
   - Observer/Message-Queue: inbox queuing for send_message, assign callbacks  
   - MVC-like structure inside mcp_server (models, server, utils)

7. Technologies & Frameworks to Annotate
   - Python 3.x, pyproject.toml (Poetry/UV packaging)  
   - HTTP server (FastAPI or Flask-style via mcp_server/server.py)  
   - tmux CLI wrapper  
   - SQLite or file-based DB via clients/database.py  
   - Cron scheduler via Python (services/flow_service.py)  
   - Markdown-based agent profiles

8. Diagramming Guidelines
   - Use distinct shapes/colors:
     • Blue rectangles for services (CLI, MCP Server, Scheduler)  
     • Green cylinders for databases/state stores  
     • Orange parallelograms for external adapters/providers  
     • Gray boxes for tmux session/runtime environments  
   - Label all components clearly.  
   - Use solid arrows for synchronous calls (e.g., CLI → Server).  
   - Use dashed arrows for asynchronous flows (assign, message queue).  
   - Annotate arrow lines with the type of interaction (REST call, tmux spawn, HTTP callback).  
   - Group related modules in boundary boxes (e.g., “src/cli_agent_orchestrator/services”).

9. Tailoring to CAO
   - Emphasize the CLI ↔ MCP Server boundary.  
   - Show the tmux orchestration loop: Server → tmux spawn → agent process → Server.  
   - Highlight the three orchestration patterns as annotated flows on the diagram.  
   - Include a “Flows Scheduler” sub-component under MCP Server to show cron-based triggers.

10. Essential Diagram Elements to Include
   - Component Boxes:
     • CLI Front-end  
     • MCP HTTP Server  
     • Database/State Store  
     • tmux Session Manager  
     • Agent Runtime Environments  
     • Scheduler (Flows)  
     • External Provider Adapters  
   - Arrows with direction and labels:
     • “REST API: /sessions, /messages”  
     • “tmux create-session & send keys”  
     • “DB read/write”  
     • “handoff/assign/send_message HTTP calls”  
   - Color coding or distinct shapes to separate core vs. external vs. runtime.

By following these steps and layering the components as described, you will produce a clear, accurate, and detailed system design diagram of the CLI Agent Orchestrator that reflects its modular architecture, data flows, and orchestration patterns.
